description: Six curated learning journeys; these are navigation and reflection guides, not additional coursework.

journeys.title: From stakeholder need to testable requirements
journeys.description: Practice turning an ambiguous service request into a defensible engineering obligation.
journeys.outcome: Explain the system boundary, name the stakeholder conflict, and propose a testable obligation.
journeys.prompt: Can you state which stakeholder needs are excluded and how those exclusions affect acceptance?

steps.label: Define the system and its boundaries
steps.why: How a mission-driven system boundary changes the claims, interfaces, and evidence that matter.

steps.label: Separate stakeholder claims from measurable needs
steps.why: From contested stakeholder outcomes to defensible measures, constraints, and preferences.

steps.label: Read the operational-concept chapter
steps.why: See how competing needs become scenarios and measurable service claims.

steps.label: Apply it in the Stakeholder Hearing
steps.why: Use the existing hypothetical lab to challenge and reconcile needs.

journeys.title: From hazard to defensible assurance claim
journeys.description: Find the difference between naming a hazard and producing evidence that a control works.
journeys.outcome: State a bounded safety claim with an identifiable hazard, control, and evidence gap.
journeys.prompt: What observation would refute the safety claim, and who has authority to accept the residual risk?

steps.label: Understand hazards and required controls
steps.why: Hazard identification, causal controls, dependence, and accountable residual-risk decisions

steps.label: Build a claim–argument–evidence chain
steps.why: Bounded claims, typed evidence graphs, defeaters, decision authority, and configuration validity

steps.label: Read about evidence sufficiency
steps.why: Distinguish statistical evidence from authority to accept residual risk.

steps.label: Test an evidence-sufficiency decision
steps.why: Use the existing hypothetical lab to examine whether the claim is supported.

journeys.title: From simulation results to credible decisions
journeys.description: Follow a simulation through intended use, credibility checks, and a challenge exercise.
journeys.outcome: Write a model credibility argument tied to a specific proposed decision.
journeys.prompt: Which decision would change if the model were wrong about its most sensitive assumption?

steps.label: Define the modeling purpose and assumptions
steps.why: Defining model purpose, abstraction, environment, assumptions, and credibility requirements.

steps.label: Separate implementation verification from validation
steps.why: Verifying implementation, validating intended use, and qualifying uncertainty for a decision.

steps.label: Read about using simulation for design decisions
steps.why: Study ranking and decision interpretation under model uncertainty.

steps.label: Challenge the simulation evidence
steps.why: Use the existing hypothetical lab to test alternatives and assumptions.

journeys.title: From trade study to robust choice
journeys.description: Move from weighted preference to sensitivity and robustness, without mistaking precision for certainty.
journeys.outcome: Defend a conditional design choice and identify its switching conditions.
journeys.prompt: Which changed weight or uncertain scenario would reverse your preferred alternative?

steps.label: Frame objectives and constrained alternatives
steps.why: Feasible options, Pareto efficiency, preference functions, uncertainty, and sensitivity.

steps.label: Challenge the choice under uncertainty
steps.why: Expected value, worst-case costs, minimax regret, and scenario-dependent technical margins

steps.label: Read robustness, regret and information value
steps.why: Learn how robustness changes design decisions.

steps.label: Stress-test a decision
steps.why: Use the existing hypothetical decision science lab.

journeys.title: From interface definition to integration evidence
journeys.description: Understand ownership, change control, and verification across subsystem boundaries.
journeys.outcome: Specify a versioned interface contract and describe how to test it.
journeys.prompt: What fails when two independently correct components disagree about units, time, or authority?

steps.label: Define a testable interface contract
steps.why: Versioned agreements for data, power, timing, state, ownership, and exception behavior.

steps.label: Preserve configuration and test provenance
steps.why: Baselines, effectivity, change-impact graphs, as-built reconciliation, and release authority.

steps.label: Read the physical-interface design chapter
steps.why: Follow an interface from contract to allocated design.

steps.label: Practice contract review
steps.why: Use the existing physical architecture laboratory.

journeys.title: From architecture views to allocation evidence
journeys.description: See why model meaning, allocation, and traceability must agree for a model to be useful.
journeys.outcome: Explain what a model relationship means and which evidence validates the allocation.
journeys.prompt: Which model inconsistency would invalidate your design decision even if every diagram looks complete?

steps.label: Choose the model semantics
steps.why: Distinguishing engineering purpose, modeling notation, method, tools, and model governance.

steps.label: Trace engineering claims across models
steps.why: Typed, versioned relationships that support impact analysis without confusing links with proof.

steps.label: Read functional allocation in MBSE
steps.why: Examine functional responsibility allocation and assumptions.

steps.label: Critique an architecture allocation
steps.why: Use the existing hypothetical MBSE lab.
